clue.text: They are evidently not tongue-tied

parts.note: people skilled in many tongues, that is languages, can hardly be lost for words

explanation.surface: Some chatty people plainly have no trouble speaking up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tongue' means a language here, not the organ: those fluent in several are the opposite of tongue-tied.
explanation.definitionFit: Linguists are people with a command of several languages, and a language is a tongue.

clue.text: Spot avoided by shady customers?

parts.note: 'spot' is a spotlight, and 'shady' means both dishonest and keeping to the shade

explanation.surface: Crooks keep clear of a certain place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spot' suggests a place, but it is a spotlight: shady characters like the shadows and avoid public attention.
explanation.definitionFit: Limelight was an old stage spotlight, and now means the glare of public attention.

clue.text: In their case, sticking out is a risky, business:

definitions.text: In their case, sticking out is a risky, business

parts.words: In their case, sticking out is a risky, business
parts.note: to stick your neck out is to take a risk, and here the body parts themselves are sticking out

explanation.surface: Some people find that standing out from the crowd is dangerous.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'stick your neck out' means take a risk; the clue applies it to the body parts.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom of sticking one's neck out, meaning to risk trouble, names these body parts.

clue.text: The less privileged type, could, be grounded

explanation.surface: A disadvantaged person might be kept in as a punishment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grounded' suggests a punished teenager, but it describes the dog pinned underneath in a dogfight, the original underdog.
explanation.definitionFit: An underdog is someone at a disadvantage, and literally the dog beneath, held to the floor in a fight.

clue.text: They mark time in summer, if not 'Summer. Time

definitions.text: They mark time in summer, if not 'Summer. Time

parts.words: They mark time in summer, if not 'Summer. Time
parts.note: these garden timepieces show the hour only when the sun shines, and ignore clocks being put forward

explanation.surface: Some clocks keep the hour in the warm months but ignore daylight saving.
explanation.walkthrough: British Summer Time puts clocks forward an hour; a shadow cast by the sun cannot be adjusted, so it keeps true solar time.
explanation.definitionFit: Sundials tell the time by the sun's shadow, so they work in sunny weather but follow no clock changes.

clue.text: Simon or Peter-or Herb

explanation.surface: Three names offered as alternatives.
explanation.walkthrough: Simple Simon is the nursery-rhyme character, Peter Simple the hero of Captain Marryat's 1834 novel, and a simple is an old word for a medicinal herb.
explanation.definitionFit: Simple goes with Simon in the nursery rhyme, with Peter in Marryat's novel title, and alone means a medicinal plant.

clue.text: Endures in a snobbish way

explanation.surface: Someone puts up with things while looking down their nose.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'snob' was an old name for a cobbler or shoemaker, so 'snobbish' means to do with shoemaking, whose wooden foot-shaped forms are lasts.
explanation.definitionFit: To last is to go on or survive; a shoemaker's wooden foot model is also a last, so these are the cobbler's (old 'snob's') tools.

clue.text: Summer wear at school'?

parts.note: in hot weather one wears ..., and split that way the phrase gives a period of teaching

explanation.surface: A question about the uniform pupils wear in hot weather.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as 'less on', the word describes how little people wear in summer; whole, it is a class at school.
explanation.definitionFit: A lesson is a period of teaching in a school timetable.

clue.text: Fellow craftsmen

parts.note: 'craft' is read as a boat, so these are fellow men aboard one vessel

explanation.surface: Colleagues in a skilled trade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Craftsmen' suggests artisans, but a craft is a vessel: men on the same boat.
explanation.definitionFit: Shipmates are sailors serving together on the same vessel.

clue.text: Wool may 'appear flighty in an, anserine context.

definitions.text: may 'appear flighty in an, anserine context

explanation.surface: Yarn could look frivolous next to geese.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Anserine' means to do with geese: a flight of wild geese in the air is called a skein, as is a loosely coiled length of yarn.
explanation.definitionFit: A skein is a coil of yarn, and also the collective noun for wild geese in flight.

clue.text: Here was Alexander with Cromwell's bauble to put on

parts.note: Oliver Cromwell dismissed Parliament's ceremonial mace with 'take away that bauble'
to don clothes is to put them on

explanation.surface: Alexander the Great dons Cromwell's trinket.
explanation.walkthrough: Cromwell, dismissing the Rump Parliament in 1653, called the Speaker's mace 'that bauble'. Alexander the Great was king of Macedon.
explanation.definitionFit: Alexander the Great came from the ancient kingdom of Macedon, in northern Greece.

clue.text: Does it go off the target by three-quarters of a mile ?

definitions.text: Does it go off the target by three-quarters of a mile

parts.note: to go off the target is to miss it

indicators.note: three of the four letters of the word mile are kept, its last three

explanation.surface: A rocket may stray from its mark by most of a mile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'three-quarters of' keeps three of the four letters of 'mile', the last three: ILE.
explanation.definitionFit: A missile is a weapon fired at a target, which may hit or go wide of it.

clue.text: One on the beaten track?

parts.note: 'beaten' is read as defeated, so a runner on the track who has been beaten

explanation.surface: A rambler sticks to the well-trodden path.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beaten track' suggests a well-worn path, but 'beaten' means defeated: a runner who has lost the race.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who has been beaten in a race or contest has lost it.

clue.text: Remarkable if no males can be found here

indicators.note: remarkable suggests something notable, here letters to be remarked, that is marked out again in a new order

explanation.surface: It would be extraordinary to find a place with no men in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Remarkable' signals a rearrangement of IFNOMALES. The ISLE OF MAN, an island in the Irish Sea, is named after its males, ironically.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Here' stands for a place, and the island in the Irish Sea is one whose name contains men.

clue.text: One that gives an ugly look and stony stare

definitions.text: One that gives an ugly look and stony stare

parts.words: One that gives an ugly look and stony stare
parts.note: 'stony' is literal: a grotesque carved stone face on a church roof stares out

explanation.surface: Someone glares at another with a hard, unpleasant expression.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stony stare' sounds like a cold glare, but here the face is actually carved in stone.
explanation.definitionFit: A grotesque carved figure, often a waterspout on a cathedral roof, glares down in stone.

clue.text: Holding back one form of transport among the others

indicators.note: one piece sits among, that is within, the letters of the other

parts.note: the rest means the others
a train is one way of travelling

explanation.surface: Keeping one kind of vehicle in reserve while the others go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'among' puts TRAIN inside REST, between RES and T.
explanation.definitionFit: Restraint is the act of keeping something in check, a holding back.

clue.text: Steer the little ones back

indicators.note: the word supplied by the little ones is read back to front

parts.note: tots are small children

explanation.surface: Guide the youngsters home again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Steer' looks like a verb, but it is the noun: a young bullock, which in Scots and northern dialect is a stot.
explanation.definitionFit: A stot is a dialect word for a young castrated ox or bullock.

clue.text: Slang name for workers at the Royal .Mint ?

definitions.text: Slang name for workers at the Royal .Mint

parts.words: Slang name for workers at the Royal .Mint
parts.note: 'tin' is old slang for money, so makers of money are tin workers

explanation.surface: What do people call the staff who make Britain's coins?
explanation.walkthrough: The Royal Mint makes Britain's coins, and 'tin' is old British slang for cash.
explanation.definitionFit: Tinsmiths are metalworkers in tin, and tin is slang for money, which the Mint produces.

clue.text: Giving a lift ? Go in this for a change

indicators.note: the words go in this are altered, their letters reordered

explanation.surface: Offering someone a ride, and suggesting a new vehicle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for a change' signals a rearrangement of GOINTHIS.
explanation.definitionFit: Hoisting means raising or lifting something up, often with ropes.

clue.text: In stress I had caused a mishap

indicators.note: one piece goes in another, inside its letters

parts.note: an accent is stress laid on a syllable
I'd is the contraction of I had

explanation.surface: Under pressure, someone confesses to causing an unfortunate event.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' puts ID inside ACCENT, after ACC.
explanation.definitionFit: An accident is an unplanned and unfortunate event.

clue.text: Did Cowper find it a job to write it?

definitions.text: Did Cowper find it a job to write it?

parts.words: Did Cowper find it a job to write it
parts.note: William Cowper wrote a long blank-verse poem whose title is a word meaning a job

explanation.surface: Was writing it hard work for the poet Cowper?
explanation.walkthrough: William Cowper, an 18th-century English poet, wrote 'The Task' (1785); the job and the poem share the name.
explanation.definitionFit: A task is a job, and The Task is the title of Cowper's best-known poem.

clue.text: Black foot wear (in two words) ?

parts.note: joined up, Blackfoot names a Native American people, and footwear is what they put on their feet

explanation.surface: Dark shoes are described in two words.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as 'Blackfoot wear': the Blackfoot are a Native American people whose soft leather shoe is the moccasin.
explanation.definitionFit: A moccasin is the soft leather slipper-like shoe of North American peoples such as the Blackfoot.

clue.text: An artist might consider it a' blot on the landscape

definitions.text: An artist might consider it a' blot on the landscape

parts.words: An artist might consider it a' blot on the landscape
parts.note: 'blot on the landscape' is literal: a smear of paint spoiling a painted scene

explanation.surface: A painter thinks some new building spoils the view.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blot on the landscape' usually means an eyesore, but here it is an actual smear on a painted landscape.
explanation.definitionFit: A smudge is a smear or blurred mark that spoils a painting.

clue.text: Those, who go out looking for trouble, perhaps'

definitions.text: Those, who go out looking for trouble, perhaps

parts.words: Those, who go out looking for trouble, perhaps
parts.note: troublemakers seek trouble, but guards on their rounds look out for it to stop it

explanation.surface: Some people go out deliberately to start fights.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Looking for trouble' suggests troublemakers, but a group of police or soldiers on a round searches for it to prevent it.
explanation.definitionFit: A patrol is a group of guards or soldiers sent out to watch an area for danger.

clue.text: Tales of those on the dole ?

definitions.text: Tales of those on the dole

parts.words: Tales of those on the dole
parts.note: 'dole' is the old word for grief or sorrow, so these are tales of the sorrowful

explanation.surface: Stories of the unemployed drawing benefit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the dole' suggests unemployment pay, but 'dole' is also an archaic word for grief, as in doleful.
explanation.definitionFit: Jeremiads are long mournful laments, named after the prophet Jeremiah's Lamentations.

clue.text: Ruffle a little round sailor!

indicators.note: one piece goes round the other, enclosing it

parts.note: a jot is a very small amount
AB, able-bodied seaman, is a sailor

explanation.surface: Tousle the hair of a small seaman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruffle' looks like a verb, but it is a frill. 'round' puts JOT around AB, after the J.
explanation.definitionFit: A jabot is an ornamental frill or ruffle on the front of a shirt.

clue.text: Belief that one gets all the tricks.

parts.note: the Roman numeral I is one
in bridge, winning all the tricks is a grand slam

explanation.surface: A card player believes they will take every trick.
explanation.walkthrough: In bridge, taking every trick in a hand is a slam.
explanation.definitionFit: Islam is a religious faith, a system of belief founded on the teachings of Muhammad.

clue.text: Permission to: take a number into shelter.

indicators.note: one piece is taken into the other, inside it

parts.note: the lee is the sheltered side, away from the wind
V is the Roman numeral five, a number

explanation.surface: Being allowed to bring several people indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'into' puts A and V inside LEE, between L and E.
explanation.definitionFit: Leave is permission, as in leave to speak or leave of absence.

clue.text: He may put up with a good deal?

definitions.text: He may put up with a good deal?

parts.words: He may put up with a good deal
parts.note: 'put up' means erect, and 'deal' is softwood timber

explanation.surface: A tolerant man will put up with a lot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put up with a good deal' sounds like tolerance, but 'deal' is pine or fir timber and 'put up' means erect.
explanation.definitionFit: A builder puts up houses, often using deal, a cheap softwood timber.

clue.text: Nice tax dodge? Not quite correct

indicators.note: a dodge is a trick or evasion, so these letters are moved about to evade their order

explanation.surface: A neat tax avoidance scheme is slightly improper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dodge' signals the rearrangement of NICETAX.
explanation.definitionFit: Inexact means imprecise or not entirely accurate.

clue.text: In this part he gets the bird first.

indicators.note: the bird comes first, before the word he, so the charade starts with it

parts.note: a tit is a small songbird
taken as written

explanation.surface: In this role the actor is first to be hissed off stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gets the bird' hints at a booed performer, but it is the TIT placed first, before HE. A tithe was the tenth part of produce paid to the church.
explanation.definitionFit: A tithe is a tenth part of one's income or produce, once paid to the church.

clue.text: Added "to cakes by self-raising flour?

parts.note: flour that rises on its own makes a cake airy, which is what it adds

explanation.surface: Something a baker's flour puts into sponges.
explanation.walkthrough: Self-raising flour contains a raising agent, so the cakes come out airy rather than heavy.
explanation.definitionFit: Lightness is the quality of being airy and not dense, which raising agents give a cake.
